title: Creating the Transfer Functionality
summary: Builds the Motoko transfer function that moves tokens between two principals, after a short demo showing that msg.caller changes to the canister itself when one canister function calls another. Then wires a Transfer React component with controlled inputs, a disabled button while waiting, and a hidden feedback paragraph.

concepts.heading: Who is msg.caller when a function calls another function?
points: Demo: temporarily strip transfer down to a Debug.print of the caller plus a call to payOut(), then run dfx deploy and trigger each path to compare the printed principal.
Calling payOut from the command line (dfx canister call <canister> payOut) prints the principal of the identity controlling the terminal.
Calling payOut from the frontend button prints the principal of the website user.
Calling transfer (which internally calls payOut) prints neither of those: it prints the canister's own ID, the same ID shown in the 'Upgrading code for canister ...' line during dfx deploy.
Takeaway: inside a canister, an internal call to another public function is made by the canister (the whole actor), so msg.caller there is the canister, not the original user.

Consequence for design: do not call a shared function like payOut from transfer and expect the user identity to carry through. Use the non-shared helper (balanceOf is a plain query that takes the principal as an argument) and pass msg.caller explicitly.
(Extra) Check the spelling and capitalization of method names on the CLI; the lecture notes the capital O in payOut.

concepts.heading: Signature of transfer
points: Declared as public shared (msg) func transfer(to : Principal, amount : Nat) : async Text. shared (msg) exposes the caller; the return is a Text status message like payOut.
There is no 'from' parameter: the sender is always msg.caller, so a user can only spend from their own account. This is what makes the function safe to expose.
to is a Principal (the long textual ID the user pastes in) and amount is a Nat.
Until the body is complete, add a placeholder return "Success" at the bottom so the type checker stops complaining while you write the logic.

concepts.heading: Transfer logic step by step
points: Read the sender balance: let fromBalance = await balanceOf(msg.caller). balanceOf is an async query function, so the call must be awaited, otherwise the compiler reports a type error (an async value is not a Nat).

Guard: only proceed if fromBalance > amount; otherwise return the text 'Insufficient Funds'. (Extra) The reference repo uses strict greater-than, so sending exactly your whole balance is rejected; >= would allow it.

Compute let newFromBalance : Nat = fromBalance - amount. The explicit Nat annotation is needed because Motoko's subtraction could in principle go below zero and warns otherwise; the guard already guarantees it cannot.
Write it back with balances.put(msg.caller, newFromBalance), which replaces the existing entry for that key in the HashMap.
Read the recipient balance with await balanceOf(to). balanceOf already returns 0 for principals not in the map, so brand-new recipients work without extra code.
Compute newToBalance = toBalance + amount and store it with balances.put(to, newToBalance).
Return 'Success'. The whole function is just a subtraction, an addition and two ledger updates.
(Extra) Because there are awaits between the reads and the writes, concurrent calls could interleave; for a production token the balance changes should be done without an await in between.

concepts.heading: Transfer component state and wiring
points: Two controlled inputs: recipientId/setId and amount/setAmount, both useState(""). Each input has value={...} and onChange={(e) => setX(e.target.value)} so state always holds the current text.
The same pattern was used for the balance checker; it keeps the latest values available when the button is clicked.

Import the backend actor from the generated declarations folder (path three levels up, in /declarations, named for the canister) and call await backend.transfer(to, amount). Method names are case sensitive.
Type conversion is required: input values are strings. Import Principal from @dfinity/principal and use Principal.fromText(recipientId) for the first argument, and Number(amount) for the second.
Spelling mistakes in state variable names (the instructor hit one with amount) must be fixed in every place it is used.

concepts.heading: Testing the flow
points: Run dfx deploy first; redeploying resets the in-memory ledger, so balances start at 0.
Claim from the faucet (10,000 tokens), copy a target principal, transfer 50, then re-check both balances: the sender drops by 50 and the recipient shows 50.
Check the recipient by pasting their principal into the balance checker.

concepts.heading: UX touches
points: Disable the button while the call is in flight: isDisable state (initially false) bound to the button's disabled attribute; set true at click start and false after the result arrives.
Capture the returned text: const result = await transfer(...), store it in a feedback state (initially empty string) and render it in a paragraph.

Hide the paragraph initially with an isHidden state (initially true) bound to the hidden attribute; set it to true at the start of each click and to false once feedback is set, so stale messages vanish.
Test both outcomes: 'Success', and transferring more than you hold (e.g. 100,000 with a 10,000 balance) gives 'Insufficient Funds' after a pause.

task.name: Implement token transfer (backend and UI)
task.starting_point: Project from the previous lesson with balanceOf, getSymbol, payOut and a Transfer component that has inputs but no logic.
task.goal: Let the signed-in user send an amount of tokens to any principal and see the outcome in the page.
steps: Demo (optional): in transfer, Debug.print msg.caller and call payOut; deploy and compare the principal from CLI, frontend and internal call.
Make transfer public shared (msg) with params to : Principal and amount : Nat returning async Text.
If fromBalance > amount, subtract with an explicit Nat type and balances.put for msg.caller.
Fetch toBalance with await balanceOf(to), add amount, balances.put for to; return "Success".
In Transfer.jsx add useState for recipientId and amount and bind to the inputs.
In handleClick convert with Principal.fromText and Number, then await the backend transfer.
Add isDisable, feedback and isHidden state to disable the button, show the result and hide it between clicks.
Run dfx deploy, claim from faucet, transfer 50, verify both balances; then try an oversized amount.
task.expected_result: Sender balance drops, recipient balance rises, button greys out during the call, and the page shows Success or Insufficient Funds.
task.reference_repo_path: Section 41 - Create Your Own Crypto Token/41.06 Creating the Transfer Functionality/DANG/src/DANG_backend/main.mo (and DANG_frontend/src/components/Transfer.jsx)

pitfalls: Forgetting await on balanceOf, which gives a type error.
Passing the raw string or the input text instead of Principal.fromText / Number to the backend.
Assuming msg.caller is the user inside a function reached via an internal call.
Redeploying resets the HashMap, so balances go back to zero.
Misspelled state variable or method names (the generated method is case sensitive).
Using > rather than >= means an exact full-balance transfer fails.
